verses.note: Because the world is declared very good, evil is not part of its original design. Genesis 3 will present sin and death as an intrusion, which is why the Bible's hope is for the healing of creation rather than escape from it.

Why the man did not die physically on the day he ate is a long-standing question. The main answers are that ‘in the day’ means ‘when’ and the sentence is the onset of mortality; that death here includes separation from God, which happens at once in chapter 3; and that God in mercy delayed the full sentence. Paul treats the death that entered through Adam as both physical and spiritual (Romans 5:12).

Shame enters only with sin. Before the fall, exposure brings no fear, which means that shame is not native to being human but a sign of something broken. Scripture's promise of salvation includes the covering and removal of shame (Isaiah 54:4, Hebrews 12:2).
The first temptation is not a direct denial but a question that recasts God's word as a restriction and God himself as stingy. Sin begins in the mind's picture of God before it reaches the hand.

The heart of the temptation is to become like God by taking what he has not given, deciding good and evil apart from him. Jesus calls the devil a liar and a murderer from the beginning (John 8:44), and this verse is the pattern: a lie that leads to death.

Sin works through goods rightly made: food, beauty, and wisdom are all God's gifts. The wrong lies in seizing them against his word. Readers have long noticed a thematic parallel in 1 John 2:16 (the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, the pride of life), though John does not cite this verse.

Knowledge gained by disobedience brings shame, not freedom. The couple's openness to one another is lost first, before God even appears, and their response is to hide themselves behind something they have made.

The story withholds the reason for God's choice and puts the spotlight on Cain's reaction. That reaction, anger at God and envy of a brother, is what the rest of the chapter traces. 1 John 3:12 says Cain's own deeds were evil and his brother's righteous.

Sin is pictured as an active power seeking to master a person, yet Cain is not helpless before it. The verse holds together what the rest of Scripture keeps: sin's real force and human responsibility to resist it (Romans 6:12-14, James 1:14-15).
Sin has grown from Cain's hidden murder, followed by fear, to open killing celebrated in verse. God's protection of Cain is turned into a license for unlimited revenge.

Adam's death fulfills God's word in the garden, however long delayed. Paul reads this list's refrain as evidence that death reigned from Adam onward (Romans 5:14), because sin had entered the world through one man.

Whatever the identity of the sons of God, the verse describes sin in the shape of chapter 3: seeing, desiring, and taking without regard to God's order. The multiplication God blessed becomes the occasion for new transgression.

The heroes of old are remembered for renown, not righteousness. By placing them just before the verdict of verse 5, Genesis treats the human quest for a great name apart from God as part of what went wrong.

Sin has reached the source of action, the heart's inclination. Genesis 8:21 repeats this verse's diagnosis after the flood, so the flood cleanses the earth but does not change the human heart. Scripture's answer is a new heart given by God (Ezekiel 36:26).

God's verdict on the human heart is the same after the flood as before it, and it now adds “from his youth”. Sin is not a habit learned late but an inclination present from the start. Judgment removed a generation; it did not change the heart.

The man God called righteous and blameless (6:9) falls within a few verses of the covenant. Genesis does not excuse him or explain the lapse away. The flood removed the violent generation; it did not produce a sinless one, and the Bible's heroes are shown with their failures.

Sin's consequences run across generations in this story, as they did from Adam to Cain to Lamech. Scripture holds together two truths that later passages spell out: children often bear the effects of their parents' sins (Exodus 20:5), and each person answers for his own guilt (Ezekiel 18:20).

The builders' sin is not building or cooperating but seeking a name and a security of their own making, in defiance of God's command to spread out. The same impulse, to secure oneself apart from God, runs from Eden to Babel, and Babylon remains its symbol through the end of the Bible (Revelation 18:2).

The verse names Sodom's sin without detail, leaving the specifics for later texts. Ezekiel 16:49-50 describes Sodom's guilt as arrogance, plenty of food, and careless ease while they did not help the poor and needy, together with detestable acts; Genesis 19 shows violent sexual assault on strangers. The Bible's picture of Sodom joins pride, indulgence, and cruelty.

Sarai's reasoning begins with a true confession, that the LORD governs the womb, and ends with a scheme to get around him. The phrasing of Abram's consent recalls Adam listening to his wife's voice (3:17), and the rest of the chapter shows the cost.

Christians read the sin of this verse differently in part. Many interpreters, drawing on Jude 7 and on Levitical law, see same-sex intercourse as part of what the text condemns, alongside violence and inhospitality. Others argue that the story concerns rape and the humiliation of strangers, and that it does not address consensual relationships. All agree that the act demanded is gang rape, and that Scripture names Sodom for pride, cruelty to the vulnerable, and sexual violence together (Ezekiel 16:49-50, Jude 7).
Her look is not curiosity alone but attachment. Jesus's warning, ‘Remember Lot's wife’, is given in the context of not turning back for possessions when the Son of Man comes (Luke 17:31-33).

Lot's daughters use the language of preserving offspring, the language of God's promise, for a plan God later forbids (Leviticus 18:6-7). The scene recalls Noah's drunkenness after the flood (9:20-27): rescue from judgment does not remove the sin within the rescued family.

The verse sets the promised son's mother inside a foreign king's household on the eve of the promised birth. Abraham's lie is not a private weakness; it endangers the very promise he has been given, which is how Genesis tends to show sin, reaching past the sinner to others.

Abimelech distinguishes guilt that comes from intent from harm done in ignorance, and God will accept the distinction in verse 6. Yet the danger is real even so: Scripture treats wrongs done unknowingly as still wrongs, which is why the law later provides offerings for unintentional sin (Leviticus 4:2).
Sin against a neighbor is sin against God. The verse grounds the moral law in God's own claim, the same logic as Psalm 51:4 and Genesis 39:9.

Abraham's defense shows that deception does not require a false statement. Scripture judges speech by what it intends to make others believe, which is why the ninth commandment speaks of false witness rather than merely false words.

Jacob's first act, told through his name, is to reach for what belongs to his brother. Genesis does not hide that the chosen one is also a grasper, and the rest of his story shows God working with and against that grasping until Jacob receives a new name at the Jabbok (Genesis 32:28).

The verse locates Esau's sin in contempt, not in being tricked. He let a moment's appetite decide what was meant for the future, and Hebrews 12:16 calls that godlessness. Jacob's exploitation of his brother's hunger is also left standing without approval; the story will make him pay for his grasping.

Isaac has just been told "I will be with you" and still lies to protect himself. The verse is a plain picture of how sin runs in families: the son repeats his father's failure in his father's words, a generation after God rescued the father from it.

Jacob's only scruple is the risk of being caught, and Rebekah's reply, "Your curse be on me, my son", tries to take on herself a consequence that no one can transfer by saying so. Both treat the blessing as something to be secured by management rather than received from God.
Jacob not only lies but uses God's name to support the lie. The command not to take the LORD's name in vain (Exodus 20:7) forbids exactly this, making God an accomplice to one's own schemes.

Esau's account is partly true and partly self-serving: Jacob did deceive him for the blessing, but Esau sold the birthright freely in 25:33. The verse lets the reader hear a wronged man's grief without letting him rewrite his own part in it.

Esau's sin is hatred nursed in the heart and postponed only for appearances. The New Testament traces murder to exactly this root: 1 John 3:12-15 names Cain and says that anyone who hates his brother is a murderer.

The verse shows sin returning on the sinner in kind. Jacob used darkness, disguise, and a father's blindness; Laban uses darkness, a bride who was probably veiled, and a groom's trust. Scripture calls this reaping what one sows (Galatians 6:7), and the narrator lets the symmetry speak without adding a moral.

Laban's agreement is a lie in all but words. He accepts the contract and in the same day empties it of value. The verse shows the pattern of 29:25 repeated: Laban keeps the letter of an agreement and breaks its purpose.

The narrator uses a verb of degradation for what Shechem does, whatever he feels afterward. Scripture names sexual violence as a wrong done to the woman first, not merely an offense against her family's honor.
The verse names an act as folly against the community, not only a private wrong. Israel's law will treat sexual violation as something that damages the whole people's life before God.

The wrong done to one woman is answered by capturing many women and children who had done nothing. The chapter shows how vengeance multiplies victims. Abraham, by contrast, refused to profit from the spoils of war (14:22-23).

The firstborn's act is recorded in a single line and judged decades later: Jacob's last words strip Reuben of preeminence (49:4), and Chronicles notes that his birthright passed to Joseph's sons (1 Chronicles 5:1). Scripture's silence is not approval.
Hatred is counted three times in these verses (verses 4, 5, 8), each time increasing. The brothers' sin begins with a feeling they nurse and feed, long before it becomes an act.
The brothers plan murder and the cover story together. The chapter shows sin reaching for concealment from the start, as Cain's did when he asked whether he was his brother's keeper (4:9).

Judah's appeal to brotherhood saves Joseph's life but not his freedom. The chapter shows how a lesser evil can be chosen for mixed motives, and Judah's later offer of himself as a slave in Benjamin's place (44:33) will undo what he starts here.

The text names Onan's motive: he knew the offspring would not belong to him. His sin combines greed (a son for Er would reduce his own inheritance), deception (he appeared to fulfill the duty), and contempt for a widow's claim. It is a sin committed in the privacy of a household and judged by God as fully as public violence.
Judah's sin here is his own, whatever Tamar's plan. The narrator does not excuse him for not recognizing her; he intended to use a woman he took to be a stranger, and he is the one who initiates.

Judah treats the goat as the only obligation that matters, and he treats being laughed at as the only danger. The verse shows how sin tends to concern itself with image and to overlook the wrong done to another person.

Joseph calls the act by its name before he is tempted to rename it. The verse shows that resisting sin begins with seeing it clearly, including its effect on the person wronged and its offense to God.

The accusation turns truth upside down: the one who refused becomes the attacker. False witness is forbidden in the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:16), and this scene shows why. A lie told well, with a piece of physical evidence, can destroy an innocent man.
The brothers can say "Your servants are honest men" because they have lived inside their lie so long it no longer feels like one. The story is about to press them until the buried truth comes out.
Twenty years have not erased the memory of a boy's cries. The verse shows sin living on in the conscience of those who committed it, waiting for a crisis to bring it back into speech.

A guilty conscience reads kindness as a trap. The brothers expect to be treated as they once treated Joseph. The verse shows how buried guilt distorts the way people interpret the actions of others, including acts of grace.
Judah speaks of avon, iniquity, not only of this charge but of what lies behind it. In Hebrew thought guilt remains until it is dealt with, and God is the one who finds it and brings it out.

Forgetting is where the oppression begins. The Old Testament treats refusing to acknowledge what God has done, and the people through whom he did it, as the root of injustice, which is why Israel's own law will command it again and again to remember that it was a slave in Egypt.

The verse recognizes that a generation's idolatry does not stay with that generation. Iniquity is ‘visited’ on those who continue in it, and the damage of turning from God spreads through the households and generations that live together.

Three words for wrongdoing name its different faces: guilt, rebellion, and failure. The same three appear together in the Day of Atonement confession (Leviticus 16:21), and here God names himself as the one who carries all three away.
The ritual begins with the priest's own sin. Leviticus never suggests that holiness of office makes a person sinless; the priest's garments are holy, but the priest himself still needs cleansing.
Sin has effects beyond the sinner. The verse pictures it accumulating in the place of worship, a communal pollution that the whole people shares and that God himself provides the means to remove.
‘Bearing iniquity’ describes guilt as a weight the guilty carry. The same language will later describe the servant of Isaiah 53, who bears the iniquities of others (Isaiah 53:11-12).
The verse names rebellion's logic: God's rule is felt as bondage and autonomy as freedom. Jeremiah uses the same image for Israel breaking its yoke and bursting its bonds (Jeremiah 2:20; 5:5).
Ahaz's sin is unbelief dressed as piety. The chapter shows that refusing God's offered help, while privately trusting another power, can sound like reverence and be the opposite.

The stanza describes sin as self-destructive: wickedness catches fire and consumes the society that feeds it. Judgment here is less an outside penalty than God handing a people over to the logic of what they have chosen, the pattern Paul traces in Romans 1:24-28.

Sin is described as wandering, each person choosing his own way, and as universal: ‘all of us’. The self-assessment is the speakers' own; they do not exempt themselves. Paul's catalog in Romans 3:10-12, that all have turned aside, makes the same confession.

Jeremiah elsewhere confesses that God repays the fathers' iniquity to their children (32:18), and Lamentations 5:7 voices the same experience. These verses do not deny that sin's effects run through generations; they deny that anyone is condemned for another's sin without his own. Ezekiel 18 develops the principle at length, and it has deep roots in the law (Deuteronomy 24:16).

Sin here defiles a place, not only a person. Leviticus had warned that the land would vomit out people who defiled it (Leviticus 18:24-28), and Numbers that bloodshed pollutes the land (Numbers 35:33-34). Ezekiel shows that the exile was that warning carried out.

The little horn grows in appearance as it grows in arrogance. Scripture repeatedly shows pride as a false enlargement, a self that looks greater than it is, and Daniel's book is built on the downfall of kings who exalt themselves (4:30-33; 5:20).

The list moves from missing the mark to active rebellion to turning away, and verse 6 locates the heart of it in refusing to hear. Sin in this prayer is fundamentally a refusal of God's spoken word through his messengers.

Sin begins in the heart before it reaches the act. The verse does not condemn attraction as such but the look directed toward taking what belongs to another, and it applies to men the responsibility that ancient societies often placed on women.
Sin is pictured as a debt owed to God that the debtor cannot pay. The parable of the unforgiving servant (18:23-35), where the debt is ten thousand talents, develops the image.
The passage assumes that self-deception is the normal human condition: people see others' faults easily and their own hardly at all. Honest self-examination is the first step of any correction.
‘You who are evil’ is one of the plainest statements in the Gospels that human nature, even at its most loving, is not simply good. Jesus says it without drama, as a premise everyone can grant.

The unforgivable sin is defined by its context (verse 30): looking at the Spirit's plain work of liberation and calling it demonic. It is not a word blurted out in anger, a doubt, or a single failure, but a settled refusal of the one through whom forgiveness comes.

The saying moves the source of defilement from the world outside to the person within. What makes someone unfit for God's presence is not first what touches him but what comes out of him, which no ritual washing can reach.

Sin is traced to the heart, the center of thought and will in biblical language. The list includes attitudes (envy, arrogance, folly) alongside acts, so that no one who has avoided murder and theft can count himself clean. The prophets' hope for a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26) is the only remedy that matches this diagnosis.

Satan's temptation in Mark 1:13 returns through a loyal disciple's affection. Opposition to the way of the cross can come in the form of well-meant concern, and Jesus names it for what it is: thinking as humans think rather than as God does.
The leaders recognize themselves in the story and respond not by repenting but by plotting. Knowing the truth about oneself does not by itself change the heart; it can harden it.

Mark offers no explanation that excuses Judas, and no demon (Luke 22:3 says Satan entered him). Betrayal comes from within the circle closest to Jesus, which is why every disciple will ask ‘Is it I?’ in verse 19.

Everyone in the scene shares the guilt: priests who hand him over out of envy, a crowd that chooses a murderer, a judge who knows better and yields. The church has read this not as the guilt of one people but as a mirror; Peter's sermon in Acts places Jew and Gentile together in the act (Acts 4:27).
Simon names himself, not a particular act, as sinful. The confession prepares for the chapter's theme: Jesus came for sinners (5:32), and the man who asks him to leave is the one he keeps.

Luke uses the plain label ‘sinner’ without explanation and without softening. The story does not deny her sins; it will call them ‘many’ (verse 47). What it denies is that the label has the last word about her.

Sin in this story is first a departure: taking what the father gives and going as far from him as possible to spend it. The loss of the property follows from the loss of the relationship, which is the order of the Bible's first story of sin as well.
The world's sin is described as a failure to recognize its maker. The verse locates sin in the relationship between creature and Creator before it names any particular wrong.
Sin hides. The one who does evil avoids the light for fear of exposure, which is why the Gospel presents coming to Jesus as coming to be seen truly.

Jesus links this man's future to sin without explaining his past illness by it. John 9:3 rules out treating every sickness as punishment, but this verse keeps the opposite error in view: sin has consequences more serious than a disabled body, and healing is not the end of what the man needs.

The world in John is humanity organized apart from God, and its hatred of Jesus is a response to his exposure of its works. Sin here is not only wrongdoing but a resistance to having it named, which is why light provokes hostility (3:19-20).

To die in one's sin is to die with it unforgiven and unremoved. The warning is not a curse but a statement of what happens if the one who can free them is refused, and verse 24 at once gives the way out: believing.
Unbelief is the sin that keeps every other sin in place. The plural ‘sins’ in verse 24 shows the many wrongs that remain when the one who could take them away (1:29) is refused.
Sin is a master, not only a mistake. The slave cannot free himself by trying harder, which is why the verse turns at once from the slave's condition to the Son's act.

The verse traces sin to its two oldest marks, murder and the lie, and says that whoever chooses them bears the likeness of the first liar. It is a warning addressed, in John's Gospel, to people who had believed, and every reader who handles it must hear it as addressed first to himself.

The authorities use sin as a weapon, a label for someone else. Psalm 51:5 confesses being brought forth in iniquity as a truth about oneself. The chapter will turn the charge around: the guilt that remains is theirs (verse 41).

The sin that remains is not ignorance but the claim to need no light. The verse turns the chapter's question about the blind man's sin (verse 2) onto those who asked it, and it addresses every reader who is sure he already sees.

John describes the betrayal as both the devil's suggestion and Judas's act. Evil has a source outside the human heart and a willing home inside it, and the Gospel holds Judas responsible even while naming the devil's part (compare 12:6).

Satan enters Judas as he takes the morsel, at the moment an offer of friendship is received without repentance. John does not present Judas as a helpless tool: the devil's entry follows the heart's earlier yielding (13:2), and Judas acts in the night by his own choice.

In John the world (kosmos) most often means humanity organized in rejection of God. Its inability to receive the Spirit is not a lack of evidence but a lack of sight, the blindness chapter 9 dramatized, and 1 Corinthians 2:14 describes the same inability in Paul's terms.

John uses kosmos far more than any other New Testament writer, and in more than one sense. The world is the created order made through the Word (1:10, 17:24); it is humanity, which God loved enough to give his Son (3:16); and it is humanity organized in rejection of God, which hates Jesus (7:7) and his followers. Rudolf Bultmann's Theology of the New Testament made this last sense central to his reading of John. The senses are not separated in John: the world that hates is the world God loves and into which the disciples are sent (17:18). John's world is never evil matter, as later Gnostic teachers taught, but a creation turned against its Maker.

Guilt is measured by what has been revealed. Those who saw Jesus' works and heard his words and still hated him are more responsible than those who never did, the principle Jesus states in 9:41 and Luke 12:47-48. The verse does not say that those who never heard are without sin, but that rejecting the clearest light is the deepest sin.

In John, sin is at bottom a refusal of the light that has come (3:19). Other sins are not denied, but the sin the Spirit presses on the world is the rejection of the Son, because it is the rejection of God's remedy for every other sin.
The root of human wrongdoing is identified as the suppression of truth. Sin begins not in ignorance but in resistance to what is known.

Sin damages the mind. The darkening is not only moral but intellectual: people who reject the truth about God lose the ability to think truly about the world, which Paul answers in 12:2 with the renewing of the mind.

Paul presents disordered desire as a symptom of a deeper disorder, the refusal to honor the Creator. His argument concerns what humanity as a whole has become, not a ranking of sinners, and the next chapter will insist that the one who judges stands under the same verdict.

Sin fractures relationships at every level: with God (God-haters), with family (disobedient to parents), and with neighbors (gossips, merciless). The list shows sin as a social condition, not only an individual failing.
Moral indignation is not the same as righteousness. The verse closes the escape route of those who define themselves by the sins they do not commit.
Evil is never justified by the good God brings out of it. Paul refuses every calculation that treats sin as useful to God's purposes, a refusal he will ground in union with Christ in 6:1-4.

Sin is a power that holds all humanity, Jew and Gentile, in subjection. This is why the solution cannot be moral improvement alone: people need liberation from a master, which is what chapter 6 describes.

The failure is not only in deeds but in understanding and seeking: no one naturally seeks God. Augustinian and Reformed theology has drawn from these verses the doctrine that sin affects the whole person, including the will's orientation toward God, while other traditions stress that God's grace precedes and enables every human seeking.

Speech exposes the heart (Matthew 12:34). Paul's catena treats words as the first evidence of the human condition, the organ by which people were meant to praise God and instead curse, deceive, and wound.
Paul chooses texts about Israel's own sin (Isaiah 59) and about the wicked in Israel's psalms to prove universal guilt. The Scriptures entrusted to Israel (verse 2) now bear witness against all.

Sin is universal and it has a positive loss as its result: humanity lacks the glory it was created to reflect. The verse is not only about breaking rules but about falling short of what humans were made to be.

Traditions read the verse differently. The Augustinian tradition, followed by Catholic teaching (Council of Trent, 1546) and the Reformers, sees all humanity involved in Adam's sin, whether by realism (all were present in Adam, the view of W. G. T. Shedd) or by federal headship (Adam as appointed representative, the view of Charles Hodge). Eastern Orthodox theology speaks of inherited mortality and corruption rather than inherited guilt, with each person sinning personally. Others stress that ‘because all sinned’ makes each person answerable for his own sins. All agree that humanity shares a condition it did not choose to begin and cannot end.
Death's reign before the law shows that sin is more than breaking rules. Humanity is under a power that precedes and exceeds individual transgression, a power the law exposes but did not create.

Sin here is a master, and the problem is slavery, not only guilt. The verse says the old self was crucified so that sin's grip on the body would be broken; it does not say sin itself has died, which is why verse 12 can still command believers not to let it reign.
Sin is a master who pays in death. The verse denies that anyone is simply autonomous: to refuse God is not to become free but to serve sin.
Sin is pictured as a paymaster who always pays exactly what is due. The verse does not treat death as an arbitrary penalty but as the fitting outcome of serving sin.
Paul says the law's command, meeting a person in the flesh, stirred sinful passions rather than curbing them. Sin uses even good commands as fuel, a point verses 7-13 will develop.

Paul describes sin as a power that uses what is good for evil ends. The command does not create the desire; it gives a sinful heart the occasion to rebel, the pattern Augustine explored in the stolen pears of his Confessions (book 2), where the thrill lay in the prohibition itself.

Sin works by deception: it takes a good command and makes it look like a threat to life or a withholding of good, as the serpent did with God's word in Genesis 3:1-5. The verse locates the lie in sin, not in the law.
The law makes sin visible in its true character. Sin that turns a holy command into an instrument of death shows itself as rebellion against God, not merely a moral failing.

Sin is an indwelling power, not only a series of acts. Paul is not excusing himself; he is explaining why the law, which addresses the will, cannot cure a problem that lies deeper than the will. The cure will be another indweller, the Spirit (8:9-11).
The repetition itself teaches: resolve alone produces the same failure again and again. Paul is preparing for the cry of verse 24, which looks for rescue from outside the self.
Sin is a rival authority, a ‘law’ that operates in the body and takes the person captive. Paul's picture is of a person not merely tempted but held prisoner.

The verses state that apart from the Spirit a person is not able to submit to God's law. Augustine drew on texts like this against Pelagius, and the Reformers made them central to their teaching on the bondage of the will; Arminian and Wesleyan theology accepts the inability and answers it with prevenient grace, God's enabling grace given before conversion.
Death entered through Adam. Paul reads Genesis 3 as the origin of human mortality, not only as an example of it, and treats death as an enemy (verse 26), not as a natural part of things.

Death's sting is sin. Death is not simply a biological end but the consequence of sin, and so its defeat requires sin's removal, which is why the cross and resurrection belong together (verses 3 and 17).

Scripture's verdict is that all are confined under sin. The law did not create the human condition but exposed it, and Romans 11:32 uses the same verb: God has shut up all in disobedience so that he may have mercy on all.

Paul does not say the readers were sick or struggling but dead. This verse is the root of the classic Christian teaching that sin leaves a person unable to turn to God unaided, which Augustine pressed against Pelagius and which the Reformers repeated. The point is not that sinners cannot act, since verse 2 says they walked, but that they had no life toward God.

The verse locates sin both in desire (the flesh and the mind) and in standing before God (under wrath). Paul includes himself: the Jewish people, with the law and the covenants, were not exempt. The Christian doctrine of original sin draws heavily on this verse, though how it is framed (inherited guilt or inherited corruption) differs between the Western and Eastern churches.

Sin is described as alienation and hostility toward God, expressed in the mind and in deeds. Reconciliation is needed because the relationship itself is broken, not only because rules have been broken.
Sin is traced to a wandering heart and a refusal to acknowledge God's ways, even among people who had seen his works. Experience of God's power did not produce faith.
Sin works by deceit. Its danger is not only in wrong acts but in the gradual hardening it produces in those who believe its promises.

He was without sin. Theologians have debated whether Jesus was able not to sin (and did not) or not able to sin, with most of the classical tradition affirming the latter while insisting that the temptations were real. The verse affirms both the testing and the sinlessness without resolving that question.

The verse names deception as the devil's characteristic work, from Eden to the whole world. Sin in Revelation is not merely wrongdoing but believing a lie about God and about power, which is why the book so often speaks of deceiving the nations.

After a long age without the devil's deception of the nations, the nations still follow him when he is released. Whatever the thousand years are, the verses show that human rebellion is not cured by a better environment; the heart must be made new.
